blocks.x: See we're recording today at the corner of Jackson and Liberty. Uh huh. Uh, was it 2200 Jackson Avenue? That's right. Kingdom Hall of Jehovah's Witnesses.
Uh huh.
And uh, what's today's date?
Today's September, ought to be September the 8th. September the 8th, 1960. That's right.
I guess we ought to get everybody's name on here. Go ahead.
Alright. Uh, what would you like to know? Your name. Name, George Rene. Marjorie Zander. And Dick Allen.

Okay, we got everybody's name down. See, we're going to talk some more about the funerals that they, that they had like ones where they made pictures. You said they made pictures? They made moving pictures of your brother?
Moving pictures of my brother and also of Black Benny. Uh huh. Yeah.
Did they take the sound trucks with them and microphones and everything? No, no, no.
Just the sound movies?
No, just the sound movies.

No, just the sound movies. Because that's all they had at that time. They had nothing but sound movies. Now, Black Benny's funeral was the biggest funeral of all of them. And my brother's funeral would have been big, would have been large, but see, being a Catholic, they didn't allow no music, you see. His wife didn't want no music and the priest didn't want no music either. So then that was eliminated, you see. But they did take our picture when they was coming out with the car for it, you see. And I was right in front of it. And then they took the picture again, when they was coming out, taking them out to hoist at the Catholic Church, the St. Catholic Church there, Cross Street from Charity Hospital. They took the picture then again. And then when they come out, they took the picture. Then from that we went on to the graveyard. St. Louis number two. It's on Claiborne Street.
Where's your brother buried exactly? I like to see his grave.

Yeah, well it's a society tomb. I think it's very easy for him to find, because it's in the first section, you see. Near Abbeville, you see. And it's buried in the fifth vault. It's five vaults, you see. It's near Abbeville. Yeah, it's right on Abbeville, right in there, vaults. They got, it's a five story tomb, you see, five sections, you see.
And it's a?

And it was put up in the fifth vault, you see. Which society is this? I just remember, oh yeah. You know it was the, what's this, Knights of Peter Clayman. Knights of Peter Clayman. Knights of Peter Clayman. So that's the reason why, you know, it didn't have no music. Outside that, oh man. I tell you he had to wake, he was walking all night long. And flowers, that flowers up to the ceiling. I never seen so many Easter lilies like I seen. I don't know who made that. It was rack as wide as that wall, as high as that wall too. It must have about two, three hundred of them Easter lilies on there. Beautiful thing. Look he was so nice, I said, you ought to be, you ought to wake up from here and see how you stand. They're bearing with these prayer beads too, you know, and everything. And his favorite suit he liked was that tan suit. Remember that?
They put his favorite suit on him, I didn't even know they did that.
Yeah, yeah. Suit he liked, you know, that suit he liked. He didn't wear that suit too much on there. And it's on the Special Occasion, anything, he'd wear that suit, see.
I know when I went to see Papa Celestan, you know, at the way, in the bottom, yeah I think he had his Masonic cap on every day.
Yeah, what?
Do you know they do that?

Oh yeah, sure, sure. They're bearing with whatever they desire or like. You understand, that's what they actually, remember, I know one fellow's bearing with his shoes on, because he was a preacher, you know. They're bearing with his shoes on.
Well I never thought about that.
Yeah, it was buried right down, yeah.
You mean ordinarily they take the shoes off, huh?
No, they put the shoes on.
But he was buried with his shoes on.

That's right. All that was requested, he wanted to be full dressed. And see, a long time ago when they used to bury people, they used to bury people with all their jewelry. They were watching everything, everything a person desired, they were buried, you see. That's why you take the section, the graveyard section, man, they have so much jewelry, you know. I know a fellow had box of stuff. All kinds of good, nice gold stuff and everything. Another thing too, I'll tell you about the broomsticks, eh? The broomstick section. Well, the fellows used to, you know, they'd meet. If you had a funeral, well most of the funerals in downtown, they would bury them down to go to the Hope's Graveyard, see, or even St. Louis. But a lot of the fights would take place after the funeral, being one of these uptown, you know. Because most of the graveyards would go to downtown, like the Hope's and the St. Louis Cemetery and all that. They used to have a garage cemetery, but very few people was buried there, you know. Very few. Yeah, and like I tell you, the second line, I think the second line was somewhere, he's around 900 or 1,000, behind Black Bennett. They had a funeral about maybe about 10 blocks long, and I think the second line was on both sides of the bank, just like that.
All jammed together, huh? Jammed together.

Jammed together. And still doing the same thing, what you see them doing there. The only thing they used to go to the ground, man, and go around until they fall down, and they'd be on the ground still dancing. Flat on their back, you think. It was a real show, man. It was a real thing. I look at them sometimes. I'd be busy studying, man. Sometimes they'd draw my attention so much I can't help them laughing, you know. The way they do, it's real kicks now, I tell you. Now what else would you like to know if there's something important I know you'd like to know?
Well, quite a few things. Yeah, all right. Who had the best funeral? Not necessarily the biggest, but the one where they spent the most money on it, would you say?

Well, the thing I think they spent the most funeral they spent the most money on, I think is, I would say, Black Fitness funeral. He didn't belong to one Nicolette Suits. The reason why I say that, because the fellas hired cars and things, you know what I mean? And they had to pay for the funeral, and a lot of fellas, they laid off from their works and things, put other fellas in place of their work and jobs, just to be in that funeral. And I think that was the most expensive funeral they ever had. Because everybody really just went, he was well-liking, you know? Being a kind of prize fighter too, you know? And then a good drummer, and then he used to be a bad man too, you know, one time. Because when he did settle, get down, you know, to be a real gentleman, he would wear collar and tie. He was a handsome fella too, you know? Nice, tall. Nice looking. But, boy, he would draw a crowd, and they were scared of him too, because he'd get out. We'd be playing shots, he'd stop and go out there with his billets and do it. And the fellas go to fight, he'd go out there and just hit him on the head. Hit on the head, knock him out and come on back and go to play about his business. That's right. That's why today I can't walk straight, I've got to walk right back. That's what I'm doing at the parade, I believe that, I believe that, I'm serious. That's right. I used to have a cigar on my march, you know what I mean? Rad back like that, like that, to go stepping like that. Oh, yeah.
And you're always rad back now.
Huh?
You're always rad back. Yeah, I just can't walk, just like I walked that way, you know?

I played so many parades, you know? So many parades, and them parades was hard at them times, you know? Because we used to play the Bulls, they don't have a parade, they're going out existing. The Hobgoblins, you ever heard of them? He used to go on a Halloween night. Well, them fellas used to go from Carlton down to the, I think one of the hardest parades they got right now is what, this club up there, the white club up there?
Jackson City Bulls.

Yeah, that was, whoo, they'd go from Carlton to the barracks. That was the walkingest people I ever seen. They shouldn't walk. But now, one of the kickest things, boy, is that wedding business, about playing for wedding, everything was free. You know they had more fights at a wedding than they had at any dance. And you used to have to be at the Italian home, there was no one for fights. And all that fellas fight for free beer, free wine, free sandwich, cake, ice cream, and everything. And the fellas just all called for it, and they just stayed there and gobbled it up and after they get high and they fight. We used to get off early when they had weddings. Sometimes we had to play from, you know, from eight to two, and then sometimes eight to twelve. Eight to twelve, sometimes we'd knock off eleven o'clock, sometimes twelve thirty when they'd start to go to two o'clock. All that bad riding, everything is free, you see they get full. And then time your people put on the wedding, I'll tell you, they'd give you plenty to eat, and make a dish of salad there. I was a big eater then, partner. I used to go to town that time. Well.
Who did you play for when you, what band was it when you say you played for the Bulls?
Kittman's band.
You always played with your brother's band in the street, huh?

No, well, I tell you what we had, we had, they used to call it Gut Bucket Band. Mm-hmm. See, we didn't have no no-name band. You see, we just, he would get the job and just hire the band, you see. Well, we had everybody in there. You ever know a fella, Flowers? You ever heard of a fella, Flowers? He used to play band. I believe he played Appetite, too.
I've heard plenty of talk about it, he goes in and out of town, I can never go catch him.

Can't catch him, man. Well, anyhow, he used to play Alto. We used to have them upright Alto at that time, you see. And we used to Morris French, Zebra Norris, some clan there. And then he would hire, you know, hire other fellas, sometimes Chris or anybody else, whatever he could get, see. But they had Gut Bucket Band. Now, any time Black Bender would get a funeral, well, if he couldn't get a parade, he couldn't get us, he'd get somebody else.
See.

But mostly we just called it the Gut Bucket Band. That was the second line, you see. Now, you see, way up in the front when they had them big parades, well, Papa Sellers there, that was the Tuxedo Brass Band. And they had a wonderful band. They played all them marches. But man, we was back there, Tunk, and they used to call that the Tunk back there. And we was just, there were all the second lines there, right back there. Right behind the band, by our band. Sometimes it was better, back, better brass band. Sometimes it was Kid Renny, brass band. Sometimes it was, some of any fellow got the job, that's the band. That's the way it went, on his name, you see.
Well, would they have battles between the different musicians in that one brass band, you know, contests like?

Oh, they would sometimes be trying to out blow on none of them. Yeah. Yeah, they'd try to out blow on none of them. See the second lines, you know, they, well they know how my brother could go up in there, you know. And any other trumpet player could play good like Ricard and them fellas like that, you know.
He'd be like, look out Ricard, look out Ricard. All right there, Rene, go upstairs.

And he had no better sense, you see, just going and playing. That fellow overplayed himself, you know, played too much, you know. They played too hard, sometimes they'd be too tired, man, at night, you know. All that hard playing is not necessary. Them fellas don't do that. I noticed they work together now, I know, I be watching them close, they work together now, man. But them other fellas look like this, boy, seesawing, boy, just rocking one fella. One fella let out a fella take a chorus, man, when he get ready to take that chorus, he threw his horn up in there. They kind of had a little friction there and iron there, but none of them was too hot, you know. Of course they got that swing, all right.
So what about the clarinet players? Did they ever have two clarinet players to have a little cutting content? No, no, no.

They always have one clarinet. We'd have saxophone and things like that. You see Jungle Casualty? Old man Humphrey, and a couple of more. It was one of the best street parade clarinet players you've ever seen. That's Willie Humphrey, the old man.
The old man, yeah.
See them people used to play the Little E-Fact clarinet. Can't find none there. Some of them used to play C clarinet.
Well John played pretty good Tuesday, wasn't he? Yeah, Tuesday. What the? The merry-go-round had a funeral.
Had a funeral. Oh yeah, the merry-go-round. Yeah, that's an old club too. Yeah, that's an old club. They still got their dance hall up there? I'm telling you some of it?
Yeah, 8800 block of Hickory. Yeah, yeah.
Hickory and Eagle, you know?

Yeah, yeah, uh-huh. Did they, uh, I was thinking about these generals. How would they lay the body out? They'd have the coffin there. Would they ever have the whole lid of the coffin out? Or would they have half? No, no, I'll tell you how it was.

At that time, it was laid out on like a stretcher like. You know, something looked like a sleeping cot like. They would have a, yeah, you see? And then that morning before the funeral, they'd come back and bring that coffin. See? They didn't have, like now, they just carry them in the coffin. But they didn't do that before. They'd have them on a kind of stretcher like, see? And they were staying there. And that morning, they'd come and that morning or maybe late that night, they'd come and put them in that coffin to bear them the next day.
Well, who would put them in the coffin?
The Undertaker.
Not the Paul bearers, anybody? No, no, the Undertaker.

The Undertaker's job, you see? That's when he'd come to bring the coffin, you see? He'd come to bring the coffin. But they used to carry them, they used to bring them from, now you see, I lay out late, I'm sure.

have baskets. But they used to have this, the sandal roll kind of I'm telling you about, and they'd come over the sheet, you see, and put them in there. And then when they lay them out, they would sit them on that same thing and they'd bring them all in the house. Baskets to carry the body? No, I say they do that now. That's what they do now.
Yeah, they have baskets now to carry the body? Yeah, that's what I see. They put my mother

in the basket, that's what I see them do. A regular kind of coffin shit like baskets, you know? But they didn't do that before. They just bring out this little thing like a cot, rolling cot like, and they put them on there and cover them with a sheet and roll them right in the way.
Well, when somebody was laid out, who would be there with the body?

The family? Well, they used to lay them out in the house. They used to lay them out in the house. See, the family would be there. And they'd have work all night. Some of them used to have spaghettas. I used to look for them kind of, quick. The last week I made it right here on, on Saratoga between Washington and 6th. They had a red bean breakfast. They said, I had red bean. I stood all night waiting for that red bean. Boy, it was good too. They had ham, bone, everything. It was trouble. But they don't do that anymore. All that doesn't pass. Everything go to Undertaker, 12 o'clock, they put you out.
What would they have with the red beans?
Rice.
Who would fix the food?
Oh yeah, they had beer too. They had beer and wine. Eh?
Who would fix the food?
The family. The family would fix the food. The family would cook the food.
They'd drink a little beer and wine and coffee?

Oh yeah, they'd be drinking that all night. They'd be drinking it. They'd be, you know. They got a, I don't even forgot, I believe the stand handlers, I believe them gives a supper when they die. I don't know. I heard. But there's some one of them clubs or some one of them unions, they have a supper. They have supper. Every time they have a week, they have supper. You heard of that?
No, that's new to me.

Yeah, well they used to have a supper. I'm going to find out. I'll let you all know who he was. But I think it was the stand handlers out in front of the town. Because I was supposed to go up and they were supposed to have chicken and spaghetti. Italian cheese. One time. That's right, he'd give supper.
Well would anybody play any music or sing at the wake at all?

Well they would sing, you see. If they were Protestant, they would sing songs, you know. They would sing songs. They'd sing all night long. The most quiet wedding awaits was the Catholic, you see. See everybody come in, well they just lean down and they make a prayer all about it and they go, my, my, my business. So some of them might stay there long enough to sit at the whole beach, you see, and go. But the other one, they keep up noise all night long. All night long they'd be singing. But it'd be liquor, you know. So they'd still sing until they get full, you know. And they'd go back in the kitchen and they'd make coffee. They'd cough, they'd cough all night long. But all that is passing off the scene. The cabs are not taking off.
Do you remember any of the particular songs that they would sing at the wake? I mean any hymns? I don't mean so.

Well, when the saints come marching in, you see whatever the bands play, those things will pop. Like the saints come marching in, near oh my God, simple, simply, you know. Simplified to something they could put a swing to it, you know. And when the saints come marching in, yeah. And near oh my God to thee, let's see, they had another one there playing. Oh yeah, what a friend we have in Jesus. That's when they coming out. See, when they coming out, the band, get on each side, see. Some are part of band, then some are part of band. And when they coming out, they want a friend we have in Jesus. Or either near oh my God to thee. When they coming out of church? No, when they coming out the house. Out the house. With a boss. Yeah. Yeah, when they coming out the house. When they coming out the church the same way too.
When would they play sing on, for example? Eh? What would sing on mean? Would there be any reason for playing that?
Sing on? Oh yeah, let's see. Now I forgot even how that goes again. Oh gee, turn the machine off.
Yeah, oh I'll tell you. Do you remember playing Glory Land and sing on when you were playing sing on?

Oh yeah, yeah, we played that same amount of air. They ain't much distant to the customers. They ain't much distant to the customer playing than there was then, because it's the most of the same thing. But the honest thing, I never did follow a band after the funeral, you know, lately. But we used to play our main song, all used to play it, Diddy Rambo. Do they play that yet? They don't play that no more. You ever follow a band after the funeral?

Well, the Dukes of Calvonia, they buried a guy down from the Calvonia Club. And they did. But I'd say unless the guy is a real corner guy, you know, Tump, man, they wouldn't play it now anymore. I don't know why.

Oh yeah, well, yes, but it is. Well all the bands used to play it, because most of the fellas, they used to play, they all used to ramble. See? They all would see the good time or you know, a little bit of shit. They'd do something, they would smile some way or another. But all the bands had that customer. They'd ramble until the butcher caught them down. Every band used to play that when the funeral was over. And I don't know if the bands do that now, sometimes lacking the hoops in the table, it didn't go out there, you know. Yes. They'd camp a certain piece, maybe the galbers or either the broad, and turn them loose.

It seems to me that now, some of the people who are getting buried with music are pretty respectable, you know. Yeah. Kind of society people, you know, and all that. And they might get offended, because you know, they play all kind of numbers. They play, Lady Be Good, especially for the widow. Uh-huh. And all that.
Well, something to suit their mind, yeah. Suit the families, my mind. Yeah.
Well, and some others, I'll mention, you know. Uh-huh. But, you know, I mean, they don't seem to do that as much for some people, now others, they bring on the blues, you know.

Yeah, that's right. Used to play all kinds of different things. But now people is cautious about different things. You see, they don't want to offend the families. See, people right now, they're different than they used to be. You see, all that was fun for people, but now today it's insulting plenty of people. So they say, oh, I wouldn't get that band, and that means respect my brother. After they left us, they tell me they was playing the blues, you see what I mean? It's different now, but for it was all fun. Nobody's thought no home, you see. Now today you've got to be very cautious. I believe you must have to be very cautious and playing different numbers in these parades, too. You see, they've got likes and dislikes, you know. Now just like when they say some marching in, they've got some fellas, man, don't agree with that, be playing on a parade on the street. But there's so many of them that wanted, you understand, he's got to fall down when he wanted or not.
Oh, back to the funeral. When they have a man laid out, what is in the old days on this cot deal, rolling cot, what would they have around him?

Well they wouldn't have nothing more than a sort of a veil over him, you know. That's all kind of flies and things, you know. They have a veil over them and some people would have, you know, bring flowers or something. Well they would set the flowers right at the head or at the feet, you know. They wouldn't set it in front because people walk towards the front and different people, because if a cattley walks in there, he's going to lead and make a prayer, see. The Baptist comes, he's got to stand up and pray, you understand? So they use that, they keep that front clear.
But did you ever see a clock at a deal like this, you know, in the old days, marking an hour of death?
People didn't have that kind of money. See, it's farming fashion now. Nothing takes a dot it.
He puts a clock on it.
And he's getting the money, yeah, sure. You see all that, that's expensive.
What about candles around the body? Did they have candles in those days?
Oh yeah, they used to have candles. Still had, that always was, them three candles.
And what are the three candles?

A lot of them, they're supposed to remember everything, God, Father, Son, the Holy Spirit, that's what it's supposed to be. And they don't put them candles anymore now, you know. The lights. Oh. Electric bulbs now, you see. They used to have candles. And I tell you what happened too, in them days too, in them days too, a lot of people sometimes the border held had to make them better people. There was much involvement in them days, you know. And sometimes, and sometimes like a fella, I know a fella one time, he got two legs cut off, and things were so bad they had to put a bucket under the carpet. In case the blood and stuff was dripping. Gee. Right there on St. Philip and Yelp Billerick. I guess a lot of old musicians, they didn't live in the same thing. See, at that time, but today, now, they can keep a body of money if they want.
Sew them up and everything. That's right. They can get it. Fill them full of that stuff.

Yeah, they take that little bomb and fluid, you know, and run all that other stuff out of it. Then they can gut him too, you know. You see, because when I worked in the graveyard, I worked in St. Louis graveyard, they got plenty of mommy bodies in there, you know. Petrified. Plenty of them. People was in the bomb, you see, the bomb flew, then they took the entrance out, see. And they just petrified. It was a piece of mommy. You used to work in St. Louis?
Yeah, I worked in St. Louis graveyard.
We were in there too, working in St. Louis graveyard.
Doing what?
We used to whitewash tubes. Yeah, we used to whitewash tubes. Didn't tell you that either. No. Some do, yeah. That much work? Wow. Yes, sir.
We? Working for the section? Yeah, we was working for the section, you see.
Then he got me a job in there hustling around, you see. Had to pay two and a half of permits, you see, to the priest.
You see, the priest owned them graveyards, you know.
St. Louis number one, number two, number three. And we working there. Things were a little kind of tight then, you know. When was this? I was in there.
When was this? That was in there.
Let's see, I think that was back up in the 28 or 29 or something like that. Where the back in there?
Things were rough, huh? Yeah, things were rough. The PWA, man.

We didn't play no games for a couple of people who was scared of playing for. You didn't know where you were going to get your money or not. We used to play just with wives. We know we got our money, you see. And the dancing used to be mostly on Friday, Saturday night, Thursday night, you know, Tuesday night.
Times is hard, huh?

Oh boy, it was something. It was pretty rough. Then I went to Budweiser dance hall in 35. Me and René went to that 35. Who was there at the Budweiser? Budweiser dance hall? Right there next to La Vida. You remember? Yeah, but I mean, who was with you? You had René? Me, René, Ducaugier, Ducaugier on piano, Butler rap, Gaillier they call guitar. Yeah. And Spurt on saxophone, played saxophone. Austin Young's brother? Austin Young's brother? Yeah, Austin Young's play trombone. Oh, he was there. And Eddie Handy played bass. That was his name, Eddie Handy?
Sylvester.
Sylvester Handy. Eddie Handy's brother, the one who played bass. Well, John Handy played saxophone and clarinet. Yes, he played clarinet and saxophone.

Yeah, that's John. Yeah. And then there's one who plays guitar whose name I can't think of, Julius. Well, no, no, no. And Sylvester plays bass, but they may call him Eddie, I don't know, his real name is Sylvester.
Sylvester. Yeah, that's what he liked to hear.
And I didn't get this straight. What relation was Austin Young to Spurt? I didn't get it. Spurt was his cousin or brother or something?
His brother? His brother, yeah.

Oh, yeah, it's Lester who's the cousin I think. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Lester and the kid drummer, his name begins with an L, Leon. Leon, yeah. Lee and Lester, they're two brothers. Uh-huh. And they're cousins to the other two.
I was a fine musician, boy, and he was a perfect drunkard, amateur drunkard. Who's that? Spurt.
Spurt, huh?

Boyd Reed, anything, he was a sight. The band used to come, man we had such a good sight reading band till the band used to come from the hotel there. Used to come from the Roseville Hotel and different hotels and come there and bring music. And fast they'd give it to us, they'd throw it up there, we used to play. We were sight readers, you know. What does Fulet play?
What different instruments? Saxophone and clannin. Both, huh?
Yeah, he plays. Did he play alto, tenor, baritone?
Alto.
Alto.
Alto. He'd read any kind of music, he was wonderful, good musician.
Cause after my brother left there that way, what you call him, got the job, Andrew Anderson? Yeah. That boy's a nice trumpet player, Andrew Anderson.
Who does he play like?
Does he play like anybody in particular? No, he seems to have a pretty style of his own. But he plays pretty nice, you know that? And he's a powerful trumpet player too.
He can play some pretty stuff real soft too, he can get soft and play pretty.
I'd like to see him get a real good band, man. I think he, and he's a solid nice fella too, you know.
He had a good break with George Lewis.
Yeah.
But I don't know, maybe he has troubles too, you know.

Fella can change, you know, sometimes. Fella can change. I don't know how George Lewis said, George Lewis said, you should be alright fella. And of course sometimes a fella, he'd get swell, you know. Sometimes he'd get to be popular, you see. And you just think that there.
You can do, just go along and make it with anybody, see fit, you know?
Oh no, I didn't mean George. I think Anderson sometimes has a little trouble.
Oh yeah, he might be a little hot-headed. I think he...
No, no, he maybe drinks a little bit.
But that's what I'm talking about. I'm talking about when he gets like that, see? Juggie. Yeah.
But, uh... Well, let's see, I was going to ask you about tuning your drums in the street. How would you tune your snare drum?

Well, now, the snare drum, you had to tune the snare drum loose. Couldn't truly try a drum. I'll tell you the reason why you had to do that, on account of the sun. You had to keep, you know, your snare drum with... I hear some bass drums sound awful on the street, man. Sound like you're hitting on a piece of wood that's dead, you know? Don't care. Sometimes the drums be too tight, I'd loosen it up. You see a...you notice the bass drum on a parade, if it got a vibration, it cares more, it sounds more nicer. I always did like a drum with a solid little vibration, where it carries, you know? It's more effective, don't you think so? Oh yeah. Accent sound, you know?
Well, they have some dead drum ones, none of them.

Yeah. I mean, this is sort of a bad, you know? As long as he's playing in time, you don't care how it sounds. But I think if a drum is tuned up real nice, it almost inhomens the band, you see? Most of them are sort of a tipply effect, you see? That gives them a nice sound. Because I know I used to chew my drum and then sometimes I'd, if we had a lot of numbers and like in G and D and stuff like that, I'd chew my bass drum to G. And then it sounds right along with the band.
You mean that's in the dance band?

Yeah, dance band. Well, the parade band, you mostly, the fellas all off on the band. Yeah, you see, the wife, because of that, played by by black boots, because he would have another woman, you see? Right behind that first club. See, the first grand marshal in the band, then the club. Then another grand marshal, the band, and the other club. That's all they'd be sitting in the row team. And five, six, seven, eight clubs. You want the club behind that. Now, I don't know about the setting up, but I think the most prettiest club, I believe they set in the front. I believe. I don't know how that's raised, but I believe to my effect because the most of the ones in the front always did a beautiful, you know. Don't be much in the tail end, I noticed that. I guess we all know that same thing. But it's the same procedure, you know. One club behind the other. It's the same routine.
Well, what about when Black Benny died when he didn't belong to any clubs? Well, no, the same procedure.

There's a, there was the Zulu club, the Tannemith club, the Dewitt club, part of the Tulane club. In fact, putting every club in the city. Each one of them had their grand marshal. Each one, each club represented itself. See? And there were a lot of grocery men, a lot of borrow men, you know, corner bums and things. All they had their gang, see?
They were marching there, huh? Yeah. Out in the street. Not in the second line, but in the street.

Oh, they was in the street, yeah. Second line is the bank that marches. Sidewalk marches. And then sometimes it calls for, when they're going to make a stop somewhere, well, then the club get on the street. Get on the bank. Second line, get across the street. Or in the middle of the street. But mostly they get across the street, you know. So they're the second line, yeah.
Well, did the customer having bums and funerals start with the clubs, or? Well, it seems to me like this.
Well, it seems to me like this.

It started with the club. Mostly what I think it started with, from what I can understand, from what I learnt, about 50 or 60 years back, it started from the corners. Like a good fellow was hanging on the corner, you know, and he would die. Well, they would wreck up some money and they would get a band and all his friends would march, you see. That's what I learnt, it started from, then I think it went into the clubs and dipped in places. But I think I learnt that it started from the corner. A good fellow died and said, well, now we're going to bang, you see. Because I did that many times myself. I set up clubs and I don't have that. Many times I went out begging and played for a fellow, played a few and didn't get but a dollar. Sometimes he didn't get nothing. He picked up money, you know, for a band. I paid the rest, not going to pay. And that's the way it started. As far as a lot of people can remember. Because that's been going on a long time.
Well, having some of the clubs been going on for a long time, too?

Yeah, sure. The club has been going on a long time, too. Mostly in fact, they tell me that's how clubs were formed. Because when I formed the White Rose, Lost Set Roses, White Roses, that's how we started. A fellow by the name of Bonte, he got shot. And when we marched there, and when we got in there, I said, I was about setting up the club. Who all want to set up the club, raise their hand up. It started right there. Got about nine and ten of them. Then I set up a quorum up, see. They say, you be the president. I said, well, now, who make it? Vice President. Then they took a fellow and had a bar and made it and buy a friend. See? Clumped itself too long ago. They thought I was in all that just to make some money. Which, that's always on my end, was the first thing I had them to do given little parties, you know? Little four piece band. They had the band playing. Sometimes they make money. All the money had to go to pay the band. That's what they didn't like. Plenty of them dropped out of it. I got about eight, ten dollars out of it. They got out of the seven. When they got out of the seven, you know, you split up, you know? They hadn't had no charter, nothing like that yet. It was too small. But after they had gone out of the seven, the man said, well, this is it. We don't have nothing but the staff here. We don't have no more club. It's the staff here over, because we could buy this money between hours seven. They're all right, they may have mine at night. I got mine. They're four to one club, they.
Well, the club, did the club pay for the funeral?

Yeah. They paid the club, paid for the funeral. But see, members is taxed. They're taxed the members. That's when you don't have no food around the club, the society. I got only insurance. Whenever a member dies, I don't know nothing about it. But see, every time a member dies, now you pay so much, you need the society as a club. But now with a funeral, if you miss a funeral, you're tax a dollar. See? If you can't go to a funeral, you got to pay a dollar. Then they're going to tax you so much for that dead member, and then they're going to tax you so much for you. And you're going to pay your dues, and they're going to have about maybe a dollar for a dollar and a half extra tax, you know, I couldn't. You see? They're regulating cancer, just like you see. And when the universe is turning out, well, you got to turn out whatever the desire they're going to wear, that's what you're going to wear. They're going to say, we're all going to wear $20 shirts. Well, some fellas ain't going to pay that much for it, but if the fellas find out, man, they say, man, this guy cheap screw. We got him a little $10 shirt. What is that? You got me, dude? I said, I don't fool the damn thing. I'm not going to be sure. Pay, I don't know when a member died. I got no tax or nothing. Pay some more. I don't buy no sick and medicine. I said, I get another headache and go drunk so I can dance. It was good for a headache. Take it, and it ain't going. I don't need no doubt.
Well, the clubs and the societies the same, or are there differences between them, or what?

Well, I think Balevalin is, they put you on the same basis. I tell you the reason why I say they're on the same basis. They give you, some give you a doctor in medicine, in the barrel, you know. Then a club, they might give you a, they'll bury it, they might give you a little sick, that's bad, they don't furnish you to no doctor, you see. They might furnish you medicine or something like that. But a man do better blocking the club than doing society. You see, because society don't do like a club do. A club can get a bunch of men and say, well, all right, we're a bunch of boys. We, that's our friend, he used to bump with us on the same call, and we're going to put on a dance. But society don't do that. Society don't do that. They just tax the members so much for that, you know, fellow, and that's it. But a club, they might put on a couple of dancers. Let's put on a couple of dancers to help him. He's got a wife, he's sick, he ain't able to pay his rent and stuff, you know. Now, I used to play back on Torchy Street, the other white people. You talking about take care of one another, white people do that. They really take care of, I know a fellow named Duffy. And that fellow stood sick for three years. And believe me, every time they give a dance, they sell three and four thousand tickets. That's right. Three and four thousand tickets at 25 cents apiece. That's right. And they sell out everything they get, everything they get they sell out. And they took care of that man for three years. We played back there. The other people is different. They give a take a couple of times, they say, oh, chef, why don't they put him in the hospital? I ain't got, I can't be giving all my mom. I can't be doing this, but that. He's going to complain right away. The other fellow is different. I don't know why, but it's different. So that's why, close. Now you see, I'll tell you about that. Now all that was robbed of the church. The church supported the burial of the dead. All that was set contrary to the church. Did you know that? You didn't know that. All societies and all fraternities are set in the contraintes of the church. But the church is supposed to take care of the will to take care of the sick and very big. That's the duty of the ministry. That's what they're supposed to do. That's why all, since they failed to do those things, the men of the religious office didn't fail to do these things. That way these sides of the zeros begin to be set up. They begin to be set up there. And begin to give benefits. So today now you have many insurance clubs and many clubs and many fraternal organizations. They give more help. Go on. No, you speak first because I can talk better when I'm just questioning.
I was just going to ask if you think more people today belong to insurance or to clubs. I mean, do you think?

Well, you could tell from all the insurance. Look at the insurance they have. Look at the building they got now. Whose money is there? And look at the insurance. Just imagine the insurance you got. You ever take a take there. You're going to find out something. Take the talks. I'm going to phone the book. You see the clubs and all the insurance. See. And there's more members in there. There's thousands of thousands of people. Why do you call it? Everybody. Jack Lee, every nationality. Lost the insurance company. And they look like every time they turn on, they're new insurance company. Just like the banks. All they got to do is have a man of half a million dollars capital. And you just put your money there. Then your money works. And he paid the insurance off your own money. He lands it out on 8% and you do 3. You see this, I'm going to just take that money in. When they take that money, deposit that money, they get 3 cents on each one of those dollars. Not issues.
I wanted to ask you something about a banque. Uh-huh. Oh yeah. Who would give a banque?

The societies. But not a club. Not a club. You see the club give a parade. And then the anniversary is a banquet. A banque, what you call it. That's for the society. That's how they celebrate their anniversary.
And so they have some good times too.

Oh yeah, they have a banning music. You dance, you know, free dancing. You know, I have to pay to go in. I'll get the invitation. And good eats, man. You chicken and potato salad and ham and cocoa and donuts. Well, they fix you up there in the banquet. That's why I pick up all that weight, man, in them kind of plates. That's big. I don't know. See, that's why I always like people to ask questions. But that was a good question to ask them. Because I never just thought about the, I was thinking about the anniversary. Now you see the, you know, the, you know, every time, you know, every time you're young, the insurance have an anniversary, you know what they do have it. And they're all great, so new office somewhere or something like that. See, all this expanding. But the society, they have a banquet, and then the clubs have a parade.
Well, in insurance, you get money, but not much fun, huh?
Eh? Don't get no fun at all. You got to be sick to get any benefit out of it. See, that's how you got to be dead, you don't receive it. The other part of receiving burial. That's the insurance.
Is there any club which ties in with this church in any way? I've never seen them buried with music from this church.

Well, no, we don't. We don't participate in no parades at all. You see, all we buried, that's why I don't want to have a service here. It's free here. See, we're all preaching is free. When they want to get married, married to Samuel, it's free. We don't charge. It's free. It's free. So many free things we do. I just come from Kansas City, Missouri. You know who I was trying to get when he was out of town? Count Bay. That's his own town, you know? Mm-hmm. Count Bay. Oh, the summer of the... You ever been to Kansas City, Missouri? No, I never have. If you ever go there, you want all... You want all... You want all to leave from there. You know they got some of the finest people on there I'm going to see. They're this. That hospitality, man, is great. Them people is wonderful over there. They're nice. Why they come?
They're all the same. They're just a nice.

They come to the house trust where they do. They go and leave your house and leave them with you. Me and the fellas stopped there. We had the whole house. They said, all right, man. We're going, you know? And everybody got two, three armobiles in the family. They're doing pretty good up there. They're like... Beautiful park in Kansas City. At Kansas City Stadium. Because that's all we use is parks, you know? I'm expecting to go back to New York. If I can get the money, I'm going to go back to Yankee Stadium. I'm going to go to Dallas. I don't know where this congregation is going to go at. Wherever they go, I'm going to have to follow you. Because always the majority is going to go. That's where we go at. Because I want to stop at Red Island, you know? And when we get up there and get a clinic with some of the boys. Some of the new boys and some of the old boys. And he told me he wanted to bring me around. Show them a couple of things.
Well, do they have one principal man here to preach? Or does everybody get up and preach in this church?

Well, you see, this congregation there, it's a congregation of ministers, evangelist ministers and missionaries. See, everybody's a minister and a missionary. And we have a school. You see, we have a school up here. Pretty close, we got a lot of fixing up. You see, we can't do like the other organization. We don't give no suckers, no drives, and nothing. Whatever we ever contribute, let's do it. So we just have to wait. So we get enough contributions someday to try to do this. I mean, I worked for you, made me a friend, $200 worth of paint. I got it down there. When we ever get the buildings, straighten it up. You can change it.
But they don't have any one head pre-tell?

Well, we have one that's called a congregation servant. Either one is the head. He's over all of us, you see. Each one. Now, my office is the severe territories. See, I handle territories. And I handle, I used to have the magazine. I handle all that. That's my, then I handle a school yard on the Tuesday night. A Bible class school. I handle Bible class on Tuesday night. That's three positions. They all see all the important positions too.
That you would not yourself then preach a funeral service? Oh yeah, sure.

Somebody would say, well, I want to request you to do it. I'll do it, sure. Sure, I'll do it. If you request me, you got me James. If I'm working, I have to lay off. Because you request that. You got to pull that requesters out, you see. We had one few of the other, some folks. One outside? Yes, sir. And one body laid out, you see. One, one of the members from the other congregation downtown, she requested that, you know. Most all of them, they, they have a layout and other tapers, you know. And sometimes some of them are layout. And sometimes some of them are layout. Yeah. And stuff
Well how does the funeral service work in this particular congregation?

What's the same as daughters? We have a, like the night of the week, we have a little short talk. This day of funeral we have such subject as why does man die? And where does man go? Will man live again? Shoulder live a true resurrection. Why man did this, this is being our first father's enemies. That's it fell upon us, we all come ashore. So we have a little talk before, dismiss the body and after we get through our talk, then we say now their body is ready for viewing, you see they can review the body that the people are passing along. Some of them look at it, some of them kiss it, some of them cry over it. They have to get through that to set it up. And we came to the graveyard, and when we came to the graveyard then we have a prayer meeting. Of course we have a prayer and a song, I forgot to do it enough to talk, you see. At the funeral service. And when we get to the graveyard, we make another prayer. We say Lord's prayer out there. And then we have a little short talk. So I'm sure that man, from ashes to ashes, dusting, and dusting, and silver to him. That's the time everybody grab a little piece of mud and throw it in the car. That's the tradition, you know. When they hear you see that, they do that, you know. Pick up a little piece of mud and throw it in. And that's all over. They don't cover up before in front, you know. You don't know that when they go. Well, they did that to keep a lot of people from falling out. That's the time people fall out, you know. They start to throw that mud on top of them. I ain't gonna see them, someone wanna go in there. So now they keep the people from grieving so much. They just put the cotton down there and put a string over it. And put the flowers away till you grow away. And they cover it up and that's it. So there's quite a great lot of expenses to, to my students, to these tapes, eh? Oh yeah.
I wanted to ask you one other thing you were talking about before. It awake, when old fashioned wakes, when they used to sing. Uh huh. Would they sing the song slow or fast? What kind of tempo?

Well, mostly they got a drag or blues style of tempo. See the Baptist, they all sing on the same style, sort of blues style, you know what I mean? Because when we, when I was playing, used to play for the church, all we did was play the blues. And they sung.
And you played for the churches? You played music in church? Yeah, yeah. I played for the church. Yeah. Yeah.

Played for the spiritual and all. Meet John Lewis one time. He got a job for a spiritual woman down on foot street one time. I'll never forget that. And we played on the outside, draw people, you know.
And you played the same old blues, huh? That's all I was doing, I played the same old blues. You don't believe it?

Yeah, you get one of them old piano, and I had one fellow pass through you. You say, you all have music in you? I say, yeah. I say, but look, our music is different, yeah? I found out different, yeah? I say, you got to go on to read, so he couldn't read all the time. I say, play me a piece, boy. And he bust out with the blues. I say, Song된 what Song된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된
heard that done on one or two records but something like Goes to Walk now that has different chords and blues.

Yeah well I mean they got, now they got some other songs now that don't go like that you know. Yeah. But you see the one that's most popular though with the people. They like their long meters. They call them long meters. They like that. So I mean that suits the appetite. Now if one of these days I'll be able to get to the little piano player, she got a little organ number there. When he's older, like I tell, I'll get a set up one each time and I'm gonna let you hear some of the songs. They're pretty nice, pretty nice, nice music. Very nice music. Well I think the Catholic and us and this and whoever else. I think the Christian kid, I think they had some pretty nice music too. I'm mistaken you know. Then I have different numbers. Nine eight tempo, six eight, two four. You understand? All that. Twelve eight. Pretty tricky tempo. Eh? You have pretty tricky tempo. It's very, well all that mostly singing tempo. Oh that pig pen was at 223 South Liberty. That's right. I'm sure you did. Yeah that house. I want to get that down a little bit. Yeah. You want to go over there and talk a little bit with his wife? Maybe after we finish this. Yeah. If she's still there. Sure. She lives in that same house. Sure.
I'm a woman guitar player. She got the guitar. Little washboard guitar. Good guitar.

Yeah. Yeah. I played several occasions. I played with, like I said, with Dr. B. Sheik. Mm-hmm. And with another occasion I played. Oh! You know who that trumpet plays? Peter LeCobb. And who did he play with? With the, uh, uh, Duncan Oedis. Young Superior. Oh yeah. You know him? Oh yeah, I do. Yeah, that's the one. That's the one. It came to my mind. Peter LeCobb. Mm-hmm. Yeah.

That was the one. And, uh, let's see what we were talking about before. Now, that's good. Big I, Lloyd Piku? Yeah. They couldn't play no jazz at all. He played straight. All now. All straight. But they could cut that music, you know? That wasn't Peter Locage, huh? No, no, no. Sidney Dersween once had the Maple Leaf band. Oh, yeah. Then after he had his own band, he always had the band behind his, maybe he had his own band. He had the band.

segments.title: Opening: location, date and names
segments.summary: Recording at the Kingdom Hall on Jackson Avenue, the date (8 September 1960) and the names of those present.

segments.title: Funeral films of Kid Rena and Black Benny; Rene's Catholic funeral and wake
segments.summary: Rene says newsreel cameras filmed his brother's and Black Benny's funerals. His brother's had no music because of his wife and priest, then burial in the society tomb at St. Louis No. 2; a flower-filled wake.

segments.title: Burying people in their favorite clothes
segments.summary: They discuss burying the dead in favorite suits, Masonic caps or even shoes, as in the case of a preacher.

segments.title: Old burial jewelry, cemetery fights and the huge second line for Black Benny
segments.summary: Rene recalls people buried with jewelry, fights after funerals between uptown and downtown, and a ten-block-long funeral with second liners dancing on both sides.

segments.title: Black Benny's expensive funeral and his character
segments.summary: Rene says Black Benny's was the costliest funeral. He describes him as a prize fighter, drummer and one-time bad man who commanded the crowd.

segments.title: Hard parades: the Hobgoblins and the Jackson City Bulls
segments.summary: Rene recalls playing grueling street parades, including Halloween Hobgoblins and a white club that marched long distances.

segments.title: Playing weddings, free food and fights; Kittman's band for the Bulls
segments.summary: Weddings meant free food, drink and fights, with shorter hours. Rene says he played for the Bulls in Kittman's band.

segments.title: The Gut Bucket Band and the second line behind the Tuxedo Brass Band
segments.summary: Rene's brother hired an unnamed Gut Bucket Band for street jobs, with players such as Flowers; they marched at the back, behind big bands like the Tuxedo.

segments.title: Trumpet players trying to out-blow each other in the brass bands
segments.summary: Brass-band players competed, with Rene's brother and Ricard going head to head. Rene criticises over-hard playing.

segments.title: Street clarinet players: Willie Humphrey and E-flat clarinets; the Merry-go-round club
segments.summary: Brass bands had one clarinet; Rene praises Willie Humphrey and mentions small-clarinet types. A recent Merry-go-round club funeral and its dance hall come up.

segments.title: How bodies were laid out and put in the coffin in the old days
segments.summary: Bodies lay on a cot-like stretcher until the undertaker brought the coffin. Rene contrasts today's baskets.

segments.title: The wake: family, red beans, drink and lodge suppers
segments.summary: Families laid out the dead at home and fed visitors red beans and rice, beer, wine and coffee all night. Rene mentions society suppers.

segments.title: Singing at wakes and the hymns bands played leaving the house
segments.summary: Protestant wakes had all-night singing while Catholic ones were quiet. Bands played hymns like Nearer My God to Thee as the body left.

segments.title: Playing after the funeral and changing attitudes about funeral music
segments.summary: Rene recalls bands playing lively ramble numbers after burial, and says people are now cautious about offending families.

segments.title: Laying out the body: veil, flowers and candles
segments.summary: Rene describes the veil, where flowers were placed and the three candles representing God, Father and Son, now replaced by electric bulbs.

segments.title: Old body preparation, embalming and mummified bodies
segments.summary: Rene recalls a poor man's body laid out and discusses modern embalming and petrified bodies he saw at the cemetery.

segments.chapter: Hard times and working bands of the 1930s
segments.title: Whitewashing tombs in the St. Louis cemeteries and the hard times of c. 1929
segments.summary: Rene worked whitewashing tombs in St. Louis cemeteries, paying permits to the priest.

segments.chapter: Hard times and working bands of the 1930s
segments.title: The Budweiser dance hall band of 1935 and its members
segments.summary: Rene lists the players in the 1935 band at the Budweiser dance hall. They were a sight-reading band that played hotel music.

segments.chapter: Hard times and working bands of the 1930s
segments.title: Trumpeter Andrew Anderson and his break with George Lewis
segments.summary: Rene and Zander discuss Andrew Anderson's playing, his drinking, and his time with George Lewis.

segments.title: Tuning snare and bass drums for the street and the dance band
segments.summary: Rene explains loosening the snare for the sun, a vibrating bass drum and tuning the bass drum to a key.

segments.title: Wives at funerals and tipping the bandleader for tunes
segments.summary: Rene describes a wife and an outside wife at funerals and how mourners tipped the bandleader to play pointed songs.

segments.title: A honeymoon brass band story and changing funeral times and habits
segments.summary: Zander recounts an airport honeymoon brass band. Rene notes funerals once held at 1 or 2 pm are now at any hour, and musicians' lives have changed.

segments.title: Playing snare and bass drum in the street: keeping steady time
segments.summary: Rene says he mostly played snare and sometimes bass. He prided himself on steady time and not showing off.

segments.title: Parade time signatures: street music played like dance music
segments.summary: They discuss whether street bands played 2/4 or 4/4 and conclude it was the same as for dancing, with few 6/8 marches.

segments.title: Hot tunes versus real march bands; Rene at the Eureka rehearsals
segments.summary: People wanted hot tunes from Rene's band but went to Eureka or Tuxedo for marches. Rene attended Eureka rehearsals and left.

segments.title: Who was in the Eureka band
segments.summary: Rene tries to recall Eureka members, such as Verrett on bass and Willie Parker the manager.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Identifying faces in a photo in the Pictorial History of Jazz
segments.summary: They look at a band photo, naming Rene's brother, Jimmy Brown, Richard Williams and Ike Smooth, and discuss how Rene's brother got onto trumpet.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Armstrong's book and why Rene dropped the A from the spelling Rena
segments.summary: Rene explains his name is properly Rena and that he dropped the A.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Louis Armstrong as a boy: bugle, slide whistle, natural humor
segments.summary: Rene recalls knowing Louis as a boy playing bugle and slide whistle, always joking and natural.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Gilbert's piano and trumpet playing; musicians who loved the music versus money
segments.summary: Rene talks about Gilbert, a friend of his brother who played piano. He then contrasts old musicians who loved playing with today's money-minded ones.

segments.title: Second-line clapping and funeral music's emotional pull
segments.summary: They agree funeral players still play for fun and the second line's clapping gives rhythm; Rene sees funeral traditions spreading.

segments.title: Favorite drummers and Rene's rhythm style on the sock cymbal
segments.summary: Rene names favorite drummers, including Alfred Williams, and describes his own steady rhythm style and accents on the sock cymbal.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: When the sock cymbal came in and the drumming on the Kid Rena record
segments.summary: Rene dates the sock cymbal to about 1928-30. They note the record is mostly snare and bass, and Rene thinks he may have left the sock off.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: How the 1940 Kid Rena record session came about; Rene and his brother's signals
segments.summary: A man came through Santiago to put together a jazz band. Rene says his brother would not record without him and describes their signals.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Recording the sides, takes and what the record sold
segments.summary: Each side took about forty minutes and one take was spoiled. Rene says the producer made money while the record's local sales were modest.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Asking after Red Happy Bolton
segments.summary: They talk about a friend's address and Rene advises him to stop smoking.

segments.chapter: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
segments.title: Bunk Johnson teaching Rene's brother for a bottle of wine
segments.summary: Rene recalls Bunk Johnson, a wine drinker who gave his brother ideas on trumpet.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: Uniforms of the Tuxedo, Eureka and other bands; borrowed and secondhand outfits
segments.summary: Rene describes the Tuxedo's blue uniform, the Eureka's black pants and white shirts, fireman caps, and buying cheap tuxedos for the Jefferson Tea Room.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: What the drummers played when picking up the body
segments.summary: Rene describes the snare roll cadence, slowing tempo near the house, and the roll signalling the body coming out.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: The E-flat clarinet in street bands and talk of finding old instruments
segments.summary: Rene recalls the E-flat clarinet's scream-like sound. The two trade news about current players still using E-flat and C clarinets.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: Jazz trumpet: holding the melody and where the fills go
segments.summary: Rene explains that jazz is fills between statements of the melody and criticises modern chord-heavy playing.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: A trumpet player people liked and disliked
segments.summary: Rene criticises a player who played out of harmony, though audiences enjoyed his enthusiasm.

segments.chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
segments.title: Clarinet style he likes: Earl Bostic, Sidney Bechet and a saxophonist named Sport
segments.summary: Rene praises smooth clarinet and saxophone players and tries with Zander to identify a young man called Sport who came on the riverboat.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet and great musicians who could not read
segments.summary: In a garbled stretch Rene recalls Bechet loving to play for a beer, and fine players who could not read music.

segments.title: Parker and bandleaders who hired the best background players
segments.summary: Rene says smart leaders hired the best players so clients wanted their band, and gives Kid Mouly as a weaker trumpeter.

segments.title: Kid Ernest, Kid Moulyard and bass player Jimmy Brown
segments.summary: They sort out Kid Ernest and Kid Moulyard, and Rene tells of Jimmy Brown's accident and the cause of permits.

segments.title: The Maple Leaf bands, Dr. Ernest's band and the strongman Mr. Power
segments.summary: Rene tries to recall Maple Leaf players, describes playing in Duck Ernest's band, and tells stories of dance host Mr. Power.

segments.title: Dr. Ernest's trumpet and trombone players, Harrison Barnes and a blacksmith trumpeter
segments.summary: Rene and Zander try to name the trumpeter and trombonists in Dr. Ernest's band, including Harrison Barnes.

segments.title: Rene's drum novelties, sleigh bells and Celestin firing a drummer
segments.summary: Rene describes a showy drummer, Celestin firing him, and Rene's own bag of novelty effects used while keeping time.

segments.title: Johnny Brown, the Maple Leaf players and counting a drummer as two pieces
segments.summary: They try to pin down Johnny Brown's band and the Maple Leaf lineup, and Rene explains union counting of drum pieces.

segments.title: A comic peddler who led the second line
segments.summary: Rene describes a jolly barefoot peddler whose dance steps the second line followed like a grand marshal.

segments.title: Second-line fights, caps and slippers
segments.summary: Rene describes uptown and downtown gangs meeting, the cap trick that started fights, and women boasting of cuts.

segments.title: How social clubs and auxiliaries work
segments.summary: Rene explains social clubs, anniversary parades and expensive outfits, and how auxiliaries differ.

segments.title: Grand marshals and the order of bands and clubs in a parade
segments.summary: Rene explains the sergeant at arms, first and second grand marshals, and how bands and clubs line up.

segments.title: How funeral parades began and how Rene started a club
segments.summary: Rene says the custom started on street corners, and describes forming the White Roses after a man was shot.

segments.title: How clubs pay for funerals and tax members
segments.summary: Clubs paid for funerals, taxing members and fining those who missed one.

segments.title: Clubs versus societies versus insurance companies
segments.summary: Rene compares what clubs, societies and insurance give members, and talks about insurance companies and banks.

segments.title: Society banquets versus club parades
segments.summary: Societies hold banquets for their anniversaries and clubs hold parades; Rene recalls the dances and food.

segments.title: Rene's congregation and a trip to Kansas City
segments.summary: Zander asks whether the church ties in with clubs; Rene says they do not parade, then talks about visiting Kansas City.

segments.title: How the congregation is organized and its ministers
segments.summary: Rene explains everyone is a minister, a congregation servant leads, and he holds three positions.

segments.title: Funeral service in the congregation
segments.summary: Rene describes the talks, viewing, prayers and graveside service.

segments.title: Singing tempo at wakes and Rene playing blues for churches
segments.summary: Wake singing was slow, blues-like; Rene played blues for spiritual churches and discusses tricky hymn tempos.

segments.title: Playing with Picou and Peter Bocage; Sidney Desvigne's Maple Leaf band
segments.summary: Rene recalls working with Dr. Bechet's group and Picou, trumpeter Peter Bocage's bands, and Sidney Desvigne who once had the Maple Leaf band.

segments.title: The ratchet stick
segments.summary: Rene offers to show a ratchet stick, which he says people copied for the market.
